title: Kalulu and the Lion’s Feast

body.text: A long time ago, when animals could still talk, there was a great forest near a beautiful river.
The forest was home to many animals.
Zebra, Monkey, Buffalo, Giraffe and many others lived peacefully among the trees.
And somewhere near a small hill covered with wild flowers lived a little hare named Kalulu.
Kalulu was famous throughout the forest.
But not always for good reasons.
Whenever something strange happened, everyone asked:
When Monkey could not find his bananas...
When Elephant discovered someone had tied his tail while he slept...
One morning, Lion climbed on top of a large rock and gave a mighty roar.
The sound travelled across the entire forest.
Even Crocodile lifted his head from the river.
“The king has called a meeting!” shouted Elephant.
All animals hurried to Lion’s place.
“My friends,” Lion said, “I have decided to prepare the biggest feast this forest has ever seen.”
“There will be enough food for everyone!”
The animals looked at each other.
“Because whenever Kalulu comes, something strange happens. Last year he convinced Hyena that the moon had fallen into the river.”
“And before that,” Lion continued, “he tricked Leopard into chasing his own shadow.”
“This year,” Lion announced, “there will be no tricks.”
Far away behind a tree, two long ears were listening.
“So Lion thinks he can have a feast without me?”
For two days, all the animals prepared.
Meanwhile, Kalulu sat outside his little house thinking.
He found a large empty clay pot.
Then he collected some sweet honey and poured it inside.
After that, Kalulu climbed into the pot.
The next morning, the animals saw a strange pot outside Lion’s home.
A tiny voice came from inside.
“Oh great King Lion! This is special honey sent as a gift.”
“This pot feels heavier than honey,” Elephant said.
Inside the pot, Kalulu held his breath.
“That means there is plenty of honey!”
A small nose appeared from the pot.
“This is a wonderful feast,” whispered Kalulu.
“But Lion forgot to invite the most important guest.”
Kalulu quickly jumped back inside the pot.
“I know this looks like Kalulu’s work.”
But he forgot the honey pot.
When everyone slept, Kalulu climbed out and ran home laughing.
The next morning Lion found tiny footprints.
“My friend Lion,” he said, “next time remember: even the smallest animal should not be ignored.”

lesson: Never underestimate someone because they are small or different. Everyone has value.
questions: Was Lion right not to invite Kalulu?
Was Kalulu right to trick Lion?
How could both animals have solved the problem better?

title: Kalulu and the Greedy Hyena

body.text: The night after the great feast at Lion’s home, all the animals in the forest were still talking about Kalulu.
Some animals laughed whenever they remembered how the little hare had entered the feast hidden inside a pot.
“That Kalulu!” said Elephant. “His body is small, but his tricks are bigger than the forest.”
Monkey laughed loudly from the tree.
“If Kalulu’s ears are nearby, keep your food far away!”
Hyena sat alone near a dry tree looking unhappy.
In the morning, he was hungry.
In the afternoon, he was hungry.
Even after eating, Hyena complained that he was hungry.
“Why does everyone laugh with Kalulu?” Hyena asked himself. “Why does everyone like him? I am bigger. I am stronger. I have sharper teeth.”
Hyena looked at his reflection in a small pool of water.
But there was one thing Hyena did not understand.
The animals did not remember Kalulu because he was strong.
They remembered him because he was clever.
One hot afternoon, Kalulu decided to visit the other side of the forest.
He packed a small bag with groundnuts and some wild fruits.
As he walked along the dusty path, he heard a voice behind him.
“Where are you going, my clever friend?”
Whenever Hyena called someone his friend, he normally wanted something.
“I am just taking a walk,” answered Kalulu.
“A walk?” Hyena replied. “Wonderful! I also love walking.”
Kalulu looked at Hyena’s big stomach.
The two animals continued along the path.
“You were hungry before we started walking.”
Kalulu shook his head and laughed.
After walking for some time, Kalulu suddenly stopped.
Kalulu closed his eyes and smelled again.
Without waiting, Hyena ran toward the smell.
Behind some bushes, the two animals found a large cooking pot.
A farmer who was working nearby had prepared his meal and left it there while he went to collect firewood.
Inside the pot was a delicious stew.
Whenever Hyena had an idea, it was usually a bad one.
“Since I found the food first, I should eat first.”
“That is true. Then we should share.”
For once, Hyena was making sense.
“We shall share like this. I will eat the meat and sweet potatoes. You can drink the soup.”
“Yes,” Hyena replied proudly. “Because I am bigger.”
He knew arguing with greedy Hyena was a waste of time.
Hyena could not believe his luck.
“Yes. What if the farmer comes back?”
Hyena stepped away from the pot.
Kalulu pointed to a small hill.
“I will climb up there and watch. If I see the farmer, I will warn you.”
“Kalulu, sometimes you are a very good friend.”
Hyena sat next to the pot.
He picked up the first piece of meat.
He dropped the meat and ran into the bushes.
“Well,” he said, “it is wrong to waste good food.”
After hiding for a long time, Hyena became confused.
When he reached the pot, he found Kalulu sitting happily.
“No, my friend. Your greed tricked you.”
“If you had agreed to share fairly, we both would have eaten together.”
Only a tiny piece of sweet potato remained.
Kalulu pushed the piece toward him.
“You are sharing after I was greedy?”
“Yes,” said Kalulu. “Because everyone deserves a chance to learn.”
Hyena ate the small piece slowly.
For the first time, he enjoyed a small meal more than a big one.
Because this meal came with wisdom.

lesson: Greed can make us lose what we already have. Sharing brings friendship and happiness.
newWords: Greedy – wanting more than you need
Share – giving part of something to others
questions: Why did Hyena want more food than Kalulu?
Did Kalulu teach Hyena a good lesson?
Why is sharing important among friends?

title: Kalulu and the Crocodiles

body.text: Many seasons passed, but stories about Kalulu continued spreading across the forest.
Wherever animals gathered, someone always had a Kalulu story to tell.
At the river, birds talked about him.
In the trees, monkeys laughed about him.
Even deep in the grasslands, the antelopes whispered about the small hare who could defeat bigger animals using only his mind.
Some animals were tired of being tricked.
One group especially wanted to teach him a lesson.
At the edge of the forest flowed a wide river.
It was not a small stream that children could jump across.
During the rainy season, the water rose high and moved quickly.
The waves crashed against the riverbanks.
Large trees grew beside it, their branches hanging over the water.
But everyone knew one important rule:
Never go too close to the water.
Because the river belonged to the crocodiles.
The crocodiles were feared by many animals.
When they floated quietly in the water, they looked like ordinary logs.
And their leader was an old crocodile named Mamba.
Mamba was bigger than all the others.
His skin was rough from many years in the river.
And there was one animal he disliked more than anyone.
One morning, Kalulu woke up very hungry.
“My stomach is making more noise than Lion’s roar,” Kalulu said.
He decided to walk around and search for food.
After walking for a long time, he reached the river.
Across the river was a beautiful garden.
“That,” he said, smiling, “is where my breakfast is waiting.”
But then he looked at the river.
He could not build a bridge.
Whenever Kalulu sat quietly, everyone knew something was happening.
Suddenly, two eyes appeared above the water.
Soon, many crocodiles were watching him.
“If it is not Kalulu the clever hare.”
“You call me your friend after all the tricks you have played?”
Then he looked at the crocodiles.
“Mamba,” said Kalulu seriously, “I am actually happy to see you.”
“I have been sent by the King of all animals.”
The crocodiles looked at each other.
“The King wants to know which animals are the greatest in the kingdom.”
“But there is a problem,” continued Kalulu.
“The King needs to know exactly how many crocodiles live in this river.”
“I must count every crocodile and take the number back to the King.”
They formed a long line across the river.
The crocodiles had created a perfect bridge.
He jumped onto the first crocodile.
Nobody wanted to spoil the counting.
Kalulu landed safely on the other side of the river.
“Enough to help me cross the river!”
The river shook with angry crocodile voices.
Kalulu picked up a sweet potato from the garden.
“My friends, you said nobody could trick you.”
“You were so busy thinking about your greatness that you forgot to ask questions.”
Later that evening, when Kalulu returned home, the animals heard what had happened.
Monkey laughed until he nearly fell from the tree.
But the oldest tortoise spoke wisely.
“Strength is useful. But pride can make even the strongest person foolish.”
And across the river, even Mamba remembered those words.
From that day forward, whenever someone praised him too much, he first stopped and thought:
“Am I being wise, or am I becoming proud?”

lesson: Being strong or powerful is good, but wisdom and humility are even more important.
newWords: Pride – thinking too highly of yourself
Recognize – to notice or appreciate something
questions: Why did the crocodiles believe Kalulu?
Was Kalulu clever or dishonest?
What happens when people become too proud?
How can strength and wisdom work together?

title: Kalulu and the Farmer’s Trap

body.text: The heavy clouds that once covered the sky had disappeared, and the warm sun now shone brightly over the land.
Everywhere you looked, the world was full of life.
The birds sang from the trees.
And the farmers smiled as they looked across their fields.
It had been a good farming season.
In one village near the edge of the forest lived an old farmer named Ba Simukonda.
Every morning before sunrise, while most people were still sleeping, Ba Simukonda was already awake.
Then he walked to his garden.
People travelled from nearby villages just to see it.
There were rows of maize standing tall.
There were pumpkins lying on the ground.
There were tomatoes shining red in the sunlight.
Unfortunately, someone else also knew about the sweet potatoes.
One morning, Ba Simukonda entered his garden carrying his basket.
“Today I will harvest some sweet potatoes for my grandchildren,” he said.
He walked to the sweet potato field.
There was a hole in the ground.
One plant had been pulled out.
On the soft ground were tiny footprints.
“This little hare thinks he is clever.”
“But this time, I will catch him.”
That evening, when the moon appeared, two long ears appeared from behind a bush.
He pulled out one sweet potato.
“This farmer grows the best sweet potatoes in the whole land.”
Kalulu looked at the empty spaces.
He picked up another sweet potato.
“But by then I will be far away.”
And he disappeared into the forest.
The next morning, Ba Simukonda returned.
This time he did not get angry.
“Today,” he said, “I will also make a trick.”
By sunset, the trap was ready.
A large basket was placed above the ground.
Under the basket he placed the biggest sweet potato from the field.
The next day Kalulu was walking through the forest when he met Monkey.
Monkey was sitting in a tree eating wild fruits.
“I know where there is plenty of food.”
“The sweetest sweet potatoes you have ever tasted.”
He remembered seeing something strange in the farmer’s garden.
But he wanted to know for sure.
When they reached the garden, Monkey saw the sweet potato under the basket.
“My friend, since you saw it first, you should have it.”
“Maybe explain that you were only checking if the trap worked.”
But Kalulu was already running away.
“I was expecting someone with long ears.”
For once, he did not laugh.
“A clever person should use wisdom to help friends, not put them in danger.”
From that day, Kalulu still remained clever…
but he slowly learned that cleverness without kindness could hurt others.

lesson: Being clever is good, but wisdom must always go together with kindness.
newWords: Trap – something used to catch someone or something
Harvest – collecting crops after they grow
Suspect – to think something might be wrong
questions: Was Kalulu right to use Monkey?
Why did the farmer forgive Monkey?
Can cleverness become a bad thing?

title: Kalulu and the Elephant’s Challenge

body.text: In the great forest where Kalulu lived, every animal had something special.
Bird could fly higher than anyone else.
Cheetah could run faster than anyone else.
Monkey could climb the tallest trees.
When a tree fell across the path, the animals called Elephant.
When a heavy rock blocked the river, they called Elephant.
When something big needed to be carried, everyone shouted:
But sometimes Elephant had one problem.
He became too proud of his strength.
One morning, all the animals gathered near the watering hole.
The butterflies flew from flower to flower.
The animals drank water and talked happily.
Suddenly Elephant lifted a huge log with his trunk.
“I am indeed the strongest animal in this forest.”
“With my strength, I can do anything.”
Old Tortoise slowly raised his head.
“Strength is important, my friend. But it is not everything.”
“What can be more important than strength?”
Then Elephant said something that caught everyone’s attention.
“Even clever Kalulu cannot defeat my strength.”
Because sitting quietly under a tree…
“Elephant says his strength is greater than your wisdom.”
“Elephant could lift Kalulu with one breath!”
“My friend Elephant, you are very strong.”
Elephant laughed so loudly the trees shook.
“Kalulu, I do not even need all my strength.”
“What challenge do you suggest?” asked Elephant.
Then he saw a long, strong rope used by the villagers.
Monkey climbed higher into the tree.
“This will be the easiest competition ever.”
That evening, Kalulu carried the rope deep into the forest.
He walked until he reached the biggest tree.
It was an enormous old baobab tree.
Its roots went deep into the earth.
Its trunk was wider than ten animals standing together.
Kalulu tied one end of the rope tightly around the tree.
Then he covered the rope with leaves.
The next morning, the forest was full of excitement.
“Maybe we should help him after Elephant pulls him away,” said Monkey.
Elephant picked up his side of the rope.
But Elephant could not see that Kalulu was not holding the rope.
The rope was tied to the baobab tree.
He wrapped the rope around his trunk.
But the rope did not move.
“No small hare can be this strong.”
He pulled with everything he had.
His feet pushed deep into the ground.
“Is Kalulu really that strong?” whispered Monkey.
Then Kalulu walked out from behind the trees.
Kalulu showed everyone the rope tied around the baobab tree.
“My friend, yesterday you said strength was everything.”
“But today a tree defeated your strength because I used my mind.”
“But gifts become greater when combined with wisdom.”
For the first time, he understood.
“And I sometimes play too many tricks.”
Elephant lifted Kalulu gently with his trunk.
And from that day, whenever there was a difficult task in the forest, animals no longer asked:

lesson: Strength is useful, but wisdom helps us use strength correctly.
newWords: Boast – talking too proudly about yourself
questions: Was Elephant wrong to be proud?
Did Kalulu prove his point?
Is intelligence more important than strength?
How can strong people use their abilities to help others?

title: Kalulu and the Leopard

body.text: The forest was usually a peaceful place.
In the mornings, birds filled the trees with beautiful songs.
The monkeys jumped from branch to branch.
The antelopes grazed quietly in the open fields.
And near the small hills, Kalulu enjoyed sitting outside his home watching the world around him.
And in this forest, many animals feared one name.
Leopard was one of the finest hunters in the whole land.
When Leopard walked through the forest, even dry leaves seemed afraid to make noise under his feet.
His yellow eyes could see movement from far away.
His sharp ears could hear the smallest sound.
And his strong legs could climb the tallest trees.
One afternoon, Leopard was resting on a tree branch.
“Why do you look as if you swallowed a bitter fruit?” asked Leopard.
“What problem can a small hare cause?”
Leopard jumped down from the tree.
Later that evening, the animals gathered near the river.
“I have heard many stories about Kalulu.”
“You all allowed a tiny hare to embarrass you.”
“He sounds like Elephant before the tug-of-war.”
“Before the next full moon, I will catch Kalulu.”
“This Leopard thinks catching me will be easy.”
Kalulu knew he had to be careful.
Because sometimes even clever animals meet challenges.
The next morning, Kalulu went looking for food.
He found some wild berries near the river.
Then a voice came from above.
Leopard was lying on a tree branch.
“I was just thinking about visiting you.”
Leopard liked the sound of that.
“There is another leopard who says he is greater than you.”
Soon they reached a high riverbank.
Below them, the water was calm and clear.
he saw another leopard staring back.
The leopard in the water growled back.
He was still a great hunter.
Whenever younger animals praised him, he said:
“Remember, even the fastest legs must listen to a wise mind.”
Not every victory should embarrass someone.
Many years later, animals still told the story:
The day Leopard fought himself in the river.
And the day a small hare taught a great hunter humility.

lesson: Pride can make even intelligent people make mistakes. Humility helps us continue learning.
newWords: Reflection – an image seen in water or a mirror
Humble – not thinking you are better than others
Embarrassed – feeling uncomfortable after making a mistake
questions: Why did Leopard believe Kalulu?
What mistake did Leopard make?
Is being confident the same as being proud?
How can we remain humble when we are good at something?

title: Chimuka and the Big Bully

body.text: This section will move into the classic Zambian school-reader style stories about children, school life, responsibility, honesty, friendship, and courage. 📚✨
"Animals can teach us wisdom, but children show us who we can become."
After the stories of Kalulu, Grandmother would allow the fire to become smaller.
The younger children would move closer.
They loved hearing about talking animals.
They laughed when Hyena was tricked.
But Grandmother wanted them to understand something important.
“Children,” she said, “stories are not only about animals in the forest.”
“No. Some of the greatest stories are about ordinary boys and girls.”
“Children who discover that doing the right thing is not always easy.”
“Tonight I will tell you about a boy named Chimuka.”
Grandmother picked up another piece of firewood.
“Because Chimuka had something more powerful than strength.”
Every morning in the village of Mulembe, the sound of children walking to school filled the air.
Some walked barefoot along the dusty paths.
Some carried their books in small bags.
Others carried them carefully in their hands.
They chased each other between the trees.
School was not just a place for learning.
It was where friendships were made.
It was where children played football using balls made from plastic bags.
It was where they learned lessons they would remember forever.
At the end of the village path stood Mulembe Primary School.
The windows were always open to allow the fresh morning air inside.
Outside stood a large mango tree.
During break time, children gathered there.
Everyone except when Kabwe was there.
Kabwe was the biggest boy in the class.
But Kabwe did not use his strength well.
When younger children played football, Kabwe took the ball.
When children sat under the mango tree, Kabwe pushed them away.
When someone had nice food, Kabwe demanded some.
Nobody wanted to argue with Kabwe.
But staying away only made Kabwe worse.
One Monday morning, a young boy named Chimuka arrived at school.
When someone dropped books, Chimuka helped pick them up.
When younger pupils struggled with homework, Chimuka explained.
When someone had no lunch, Chimuka shared.
“My son, a kind heart will take you further than strong hands.”
One afternoon, the school bell rang.
Chimuka sat under the mango tree with his friends.
His mother had packed him roasted groundnuts and a small piece of cassava.
Just as he opened his lunch...
The younger children quickly moved away.
They expected Chimuka to hand over everything.
People usually ran away from him.
“I said give me your food,” Kabwe repeated.
“But I will not give them because you frightened me.”
“You do not need to scare people for them to share with you.”
For the first time, Kabwe did not know what to say.
Slowly, Chimuka divided the groundnuts into two piles.
Nobody had asked him that before.
Kabwe often came to school without food.
His family had problems at home.
But instead of telling his friends, he became angry.
He pushed people away before they could reject him.
Their teacher, Mrs Banda, had been watching from the classroom.
“Fire can cook food and keep people warm.”
“But the same fire can destroy a house.”
“Your strength can protect people or hurt them.”
The next day, something strange happened.
A small boy dropped all his books.
And helped him pick them up.
At break time, Kabwe sat under the mango tree.
“Only if you also take some of mine.”
From that day, the biggest boy in school became the biggest helper.
And whenever children talked about bravery, they remembered Chimuka.
But because he showed kindness when everyone expected fear.

lesson: True courage is not about fighting others. Sometimes the greatest courage is showing kindness.
newWords: Bully – someone who hurts or frightens others
Courage – doing what is right even when it is difficult
questions: Why do you think Kabwe bullied other children?
Was Chimuka weak because he chose kindness?
What should you do if you see someone being bullied?
How can strong people help others?

title: Journey to Tanzania – Part One

body.text: The sound echoed across Chilanga Primary School.
Some ran outside to play football.
Others rushed home because the school holidays had finally arrived.
But among all the children leaving school that afternoon, nobody was more excited than Ngambo.
Ngambo walked home faster than usual.
His shoes kicked up small clouds of dust along the road.
His school bag bounced on his back.
Because these holidays were not ordinary holidays.
For the first time in his life…
Ngambo was going to travel outside Zambia.
Two weeks earlier, Ngambo’s father had received a letter.
In those days, letters were very special.
There were no mobile phones in every pocket.
Families waited days or weeks for news.
When the postman arrived, everyone became excited.
Uncle Joseph was Ngambo’s father’s younger brother.
Many years earlier, he had moved to Tanzania for work.
He lived in Dar es Salaam, a big city near the ocean.
I hope everyone at home is well.
It has been many years since I saw the children. I would like Ngambo and his cousin Mwansa to visit me during the school holidays.
They are growing up, and travelling will teach them many things that books alone cannot teach.
They will see new places, meet new people, and learn about another country.
“I am going to see the ocean!”
The days before travelling moved very slowly.
At least, they felt slow to Ngambo.
Every morning he woke up and counted.
Mother woke him up before sunrise.
Usually Mother had to call him many times before school.
Today he jumped out of bed.
“You have not even washed your face.”
“Why are you packing a notebook?” his sister asked.
“I want to write down everything I see.”
“Because memories are treasures. Writing helps us keep them.”
Early the next morning, they arrived at the bus station.
Ngambo had never seen so many people travelling at once.
“You are travelling far. Always stay together.”
“When you leave Zambia, you represent Zambia.”
For a moment, Ngambo felt sad.
“That means you have a good home to miss.”
Through the window he saw Zambia changing.
Roads stretched far into the distance.
They passed farmers working in fields.
They saw children waving at the bus.
They saw rivers shining in the sunlight.
Every few hours, the bus stopped.
At one stop, an old man sat next to Ngambo.
Ngambo wrote those words in his notebook.
After many hours, the bus finally reached the border.
He was officially entering another country.
When they crossed into Tanzania, Ngambo looked outside carefully.
But slowly, Ngambo began noticing differences.
He opened his notebook and wrote:
"People may live in different countries, but everywhere people laugh, work, eat, and care for family."
As evening came, the bus continued toward Dar es Salaam.

lesson: Travelling helps us understand the world and respect people from different cultures.
newWords: Journey – travelling from one place to another
Border – a place where one country meets another
Memory – something remembered from the past
questions: Why was Ngambo excited about travelling?
What advice did his father give him?
Why did the old man say the world is a classroom?
What can we learn from visiting new places?

title: Journey to Tanzania – Part Two

body.text: A New World by the Ocean
The bus continued moving through the night.
Some passengers rested their heads against the windows.
Others covered themselves with jackets because the night air had become cold.
The driver kept his eyes on the long road ahead as the headlights cut through the darkness.
But there was one passenger who struggled to sleep.
But every few minutes he opened his eyes and looked outside.
“Tanzania will still be there tomorrow. Sleep.”
But Ngambo could not stop wondering.
What would Dar es Salaam look like?
Would the ocean really be as big as people said?
Finally, while looking through the window at the stars, he slowly fell asleep.
Early the next morning, Ngambo woke up because the bus had stopped.
The quiet roads and forests were gone.
They had arrived in Dar es Salaam.
The bus station was full of activity.
Ngambo stepped down from the bus and looked around.
Suddenly they heard a familiar voice.
Uncle Joseph helped them carry their bags.
“That is travelling. Sometimes tiring, but always teaching you something.”
As they drove through the city, Ngambo looked everywhere.
Ngambo thought carefully about those words.
Then he opened his notebook and wrote them down.
When they arrived at Uncle Joseph’s house, his neighbour came outside.
That evening, Uncle Joseph taught them some simple Swahili.
“I thought travelling was only seeing places,” he said.
The First Time Seeing the Ocean
The next morning, Uncle Joseph woke them early.
He had seen pictures in books.
The water stretched further than his eyes could see.
The waves moved again and again.
Ships appeared far away like tiny toys.
For a long time, Ngambo said nothing.
“I did not know water could be this much.”
At the beach, the boys met some Tanzanian children playing football.
But one boy kicked the ball toward him.
Soon they were all running and laughing.
After the game, the boy introduced himself.
Another day, Uncle Joseph took them to the market.
Ngambo wrote everything in his notebook.
Their last evening arrived too quickly.
The boys sat outside with Uncle Joseph.
“That is the greatest lesson from travelling.”
The next morning, they boarded the bus back to Zambia.
When Ngambo first travelled, he carried only clothes in his bag.
Now he carried something more important.
When he arrived home, his little sister ran to him.
Ngambo smiled and handed her a small gift.
Just like children gathering for stories under the baobab tree.
“Let me tell you about my journey to Tanzania…”

lesson: The world becomes smaller when people learn about each other. Respect and friendship can cross any border.
newWords: Ocean – a very large body of salt water
Language – words people use to communicate
Tradition – beliefs and practices passed through generations
Experience – knowledge gained by doing something
questions: Why was Ngambo surprised when he saw the ocean?
How did football help the children become friends?
Why is learning other cultures important?
What places would you like to visit?

title: The Lost Calf

body.text: The rainy season had blessed the village of Mukonde.
Everywhere you looked, there was life.
The hills that had once been brown and dry were now covered with fresh green grass.
The maize fields danced gently whenever the wind passed.
The streams that children crossed on their way to school were once again flowing with clear water.
Butterflies moved from flower to flower.
And the animals were even happier.
Because after months of searching for dry grass, the cattle now had plenty to eat.
At the edge of Mukonde village lived a young girl named Mutinta.
She lived with her mother, father, grandmother, and younger brother.
She loved listening to grandmother’s stories at night.
But sometimes Mutinta had one problem.
When she was doing one thing…
something exciting could quickly make her forget.
“Mutinta, a person who carries responsibility must carry attention with it.”
But she did not fully understand what those words meant.
One morning, Mutinta’s father called her.
Her father was standing near the cattle shelter.
Beside him stood a beautiful young calf.
The calf was brown with a white mark on its forehead.
Its legs were still thin and playful.
“Today I need your help,” Father said.
“I need you to take Bana to the grazing field.”
Usually her older cousins looked after the cattle.
This was the first time Father trusted her.
“You are growing older. You must learn responsibility.”
“I will take good care of Bana.”
“A calf is like a small child. It needs someone responsible.”
Mutinta walked happily towards the grazing area.
“Little calf, little calf, walking with me, Eating fresh grass under the tree.”
When they reached the field, Bana immediately started eating.
“I am looking after cattle,” she said to herself.
“I am no longer a small child.”
For the first hour, everything went well.
Whenever Bana moved too far, Mutinta called:
From a nearby path came voices.
They were carrying a handmade ball.
“We are going to play,” said Chipo.
“I cannot. I am watching the calf.”
But one game became two games.
The Old Man by the Path
As Mutinta walked along the path searching, she met an old man carrying firewood.
The old man put down his firewood.
“I stopped watching because I wanted to play.”
“You have already taken the first step.”
“When we make mistakes, hiding them makes them heavier.”
“When looking for something lost, use your ears as well as your eyes.”
The wind moved through the trees.
The sound came from near the stream.
Behind some tall grass stood Bana.
The calf’s rope had become stuck around a small tree.
When Mutinta reached home, Father was waiting.
“I played with my friends and stopped watching Bana.”
“Everyone makes mistakes. Growing up means learning from them.”
That night, Grandmother told a story around the fire.
But before she started, she looked at Mutinta.
“Today someone learned that responsibility is not just being given a job.”
“It is remembering the trust someone has placed in you.”

lesson:
Being responsible means doing what you promised, even when something more exciting appears.
Everyone makes mistakes, but honest people admit mistakes and learn from them.
newWords: Responsibility – taking care of something trusted to you
Distracted – losing attention because of something else
Trust – believing someone will do the right thing
questions: Why did Mutinta forget about Bana?
Why was telling the truth important?
What responsibilities do you have at home?
How can children show they are trustworthy?

title: The Lazy Brother and the Hardworking Sister

body.text: A Story About Effort and Preparation
In a quiet village surrounded by beautiful hills lived a brother and sister.
They lived with their grandmother in a small but happy home.
It was not filled with expensive things.
But it was full of something more valuable.
Every evening, after eating supper, Grandmother sat outside with the children.
One lesson she repeated many times was:
“Children, the field does not remember the person who talked. The field remembers the person who worked.”
Although Ngambo and Mwansa grew up in the same home, they were very different.
After school, she finished her homework before playing.
“You understand that today’s work prepares tomorrow’s happiness,” she said.
Mwansa turned to the other side.
But five minutes became thirty minutes.
By the time Mwansa woke up, everyone else was already working.
One evening, dark clouds gathered above the village.
The smell of rain filled the air.
In the village, rain meant many things.
It meant rivers would flow again.
The next morning, Grandmother called Ngambo and Mwansa.
“This year, each of you will have a small field.”
She gave each child some maize seeds.
She looked at both of them.
“At harvest time, your field will show your effort.”
The next morning, Ngambo woke early.
Every day after school, she checked her plants.
“I will come after finishing my work.”
Work and enjoyment can live together when there is discipline.
On the first day, he cleared a small part of his field.
The next day, his friends came.
But another excuse came with it.
His maize seeds remained in the bag.
One evening, Grandmother walked past Mwansa’s field.
“Do not worry. I will fix it.”
“My child, time is like a river.”
“You can walk with it, but you cannot call back the water that has already passed.”
But he still did not understand.
Families carried bags of maize home.
Then Mwansa went to his field.
A few weak maize plants stood between the grass.
For the first time, he understood.
That evening, Ngambo prepared roasted maize.
“You only fail when you refuse to learn.”
Ngambo broke her maize into two pieces.
“I wasted my time while you worked.”
Before sunrise, Grandmother heard a sound outside.
At harvest time, both fields were full.
“The best harvest does not begin in the field.”

lesson: Hard work and preparation bring success. Waiting until tomorrow can make opportunities disappear.
newWords: Harvest – collecting crops after they mature
Discipline – controlling yourself to do what is right
Excuse – a reason given to avoid doing something
Opportunity – a chance to do something good
questions: Why did Ngambo succeed?
Why did Mwansa’s field fail?
Was Ngambo right to share her maize?
What small things can you work hard at today to prepare for tomorrow?

title: The King Who Had No Child

body.text: A Story About Honesty and Integrity
Many, many years ago, beyond the valleys and beyond the great rivers, there was a beautiful kingdom.
The rivers were full of fish.
The fields produced plenty of food.
The forests provided fruits and medicine.
At the centre of the kingdom stood a magnificent palace.
It was not the size of the palace that made it special.
It was not the gold decorations.
It was not the tall walls.
It was the person who lived inside.
King Mulenga was loved by his people.
Every morning, he left the palace and walked among them.
Many kings wanted people to serve them.
But King Mulenga believed something different.
“A good leader,” he always said, “must first learn how to serve.”
Because of this, his people respected him.
Whenever there was a problem, they trusted his judgement.
Whenever there was disagreement, they trusted his fairness.
King Mulenga had almost everything a person could wish for.
Inside the palace was a special room.
In that room were two beautiful chairs.
It had carefully carved animals on it.
Many years earlier, the chair had been made for the king’s future child.
No child would inherit the throne.
Sometimes the king entered the room alone.
He touched the empty chair and sighed.
“My kingdom has many riches,” he whispered.
“But who will care for my people when I am gone?”
One evening, King Mulenga called his advisers.
They were the wisest people in the kingdom.
“My friends,” said the king, “I am growing old.”
“I must choose someone who will lead this kingdom after me.”
The king shook his head again.
“A great leader must have one thing above everything.”
“How do we find such a person?”
“Test their honesty when nobody is watching.”
The next morning, drums sounded throughout the kingdom.
The royal messenger walked from village to village.
“Our great king wishes to choose a child who may one day become ruler.”
“All children between ten and fifteen years old must come to the palace tomorrow.”
“The king will give each child a special seed.”
“The child who grows the best plant will be chosen.”
Far away from the palace lived a boy named Liyungu.
Liyungu lived with his mother in a small house.
They did not own many things.
But his mother taught him important lessons.
“My son,” she often said, “a good name is worth more than gold.”
When he made mistakes, he told the truth.
When he found things that did not belong to him, he returned them.
When Liyungu heard about the king’s challenge, he became excited.
“But many children will have better pots.”
The next morning, hundreds of children gathered at the palace.
“My plant will be taller than everyone’s.”
He carried a basket of seeds.
One by one, each child received a seed.
“After three months, return with what you have grown.”
The children bowed and went home.
As soon as Liyungu reached home, he began working.
He moved it away from danger.
Meanwhile, other children started showing their plants.
Liyungu looked at his empty pot.
After three months, the palace gates opened.
“A good name is worth more than gold.”
The king looked at the empty pot.
The king looked into his eyes.
“Three months ago, I gave every child a seed.”
The children looked at their plants.
“Everyone who brought a plant replaced my seed.”
And when Liyungu finally became king, the people loved him.
A person who can be trusted with a small seed…
can be trusted with a great kingdom.

lesson: Honesty is valuable even when dishonesty appears successful. True character is shown when telling the truth is difficult.
newWords: Integrity – doing what is right even when nobody is watching
Successor – someone who takes another person’s place
Honesty – telling and living the truth
Character – the qualities that show who someone really is
questions: Why did the king boil the seeds?
Why did other children replace their seeds?
Was Liyungu brave?
Would you carry the empty pot to the palace?

title: The Boy Who Cried Lion

body.text: A Story About Truth and Trust
A long time ago, in a small village surrounded by wide grasslands, there lived a boy named Mulenga.
The village was a beautiful place.
In the morning, smoke rose gently from cooking fires.
Women prepared breakfast outside their homes.
Men walked to their fields carrying hoes.
Children swept yards before going to school.
And far away beyond the village, cattle and goats grazed peacefully among the tall grass.
They did not have many riches.
They did not have big houses.
If one family had a problem, the whole village came together.
“A village survives because people believe each other.”
But young Mulenga did not yet understand how valuable trust was.
Every morning before school holidays began, his father reminded him:
“Mulenga, during the holiday you have an important responsibility.”
“You will take the goats to graze.”
“Many important things look boring until you understand why they matter.”
At least that is what Mulenga thought.
The next morning, his mother packed food for him.
“And if there is real danger, call for help.”
Then he led the goats towards the grazing area.
“This is the longest day ever,” he complained.
“I wonder how fast people would come if there was danger.”
Everyone rushed towards the grazing field.
When they arrived, they were breathing heavily.
Mulenga looked at their worried faces.
“Mulenga, danger is not something to joke about.”
“Be careful, young man. Trust is easy to lose and difficult to regain.”
For a few days, Mulenga behaved.
But soon, he became bored again.
“We cannot leave a child in danger.”
His father looked at him sadly.
That hurt Mulenga more than anger.
“My son, today you did not lose goats.”
People no longer believed his words quickly.
When he told his friends something, they asked:
But he still did not fully understand.
The goats were grazing near some bushes.
In the village, people heard him.
“He says there is a lion again.”
“Maybe he wants to laugh at us again.”
After some time, the lion left.
When Mulenga returned home, he was quiet.
Father placed a hand on his shoulder.
The following weeks were not easy.
He told the truth even about small things.
One evening, the village elder spoke to him.
“A lie may seem small when you tell it…”
“But it grows bigger when you need people to believe you.”
Years later, when Mulenga became a father, he told his children the same lesson.
“Because a trusted name is one of the greatest treasures you can own.”

lesson: Always tell the truth. Trust takes a long time to build but can be lost quickly through dishonesty.
newWords: Consequence – what happens because of an action
questions: Why did Mulenga trick the villagers?
Why did people stop believing him?
Can lost trust be repaired?
Why are small lies still dangerous?

title: The Fisherman and the Greedy Monkey

body.text: A Story About Greed and Contentment
Along the banks of a wide and beautiful river lived an old fisherman named Bwalya.
The river was the heart of the village.
Every morning before sunrise, while the sky was still dark and the air was cool, people began their day near the river.
Children washed before going to school.
Birds flew low above the surface looking for insects.
Fishermen prepared their nets and canoes.
The river gave life to everyone.
And nobody understood the river better than Bwalya.
Bwalya had been fishing since he was a young boy.
And his father’s father had taught him before that.
He knew where the biggest fish rested.
He knew when the rains would change the water.
He knew how to listen to nature.
“Fishing,” Bwalya often told the children, “is not only about catching fish.”
Every morning, Bwalya followed the same routine.
Then he paddled quietly into the river.
“The river rewards those who respect it.”
Some fishermen wanted many fish quickly.
They became angry when they caught nothing.
And almost every evening, he returned with enough fish.
Near the river lived another creature.
Monkey lived in a tall tree overlooking the water.
And every day Monkey thought the same thing:
One afternoon, Bwalya sat under a tree preparing his meal.
The smell of roasted fish travelled through the air.
Up in the tree, Monkey sniffed.
Bwalya broke a piece and gave it to him.
“This is the best fish I have ever tasted!”
Monkey looked at the remaining fish.
Then he looked at the basket full of fish.
“Why should I only have one piece…”
The next morning, Monkey hid in the tree.
He saw where the fisherman kept his basket.
He saw where he placed his net.
“If I take the basket,” Monkey whispered, “all the fish will be mine.”
But carrying fish was not easy.
Monkey did not think about that.
Greed often thinks about getting things.
It rarely thinks about the problems afterwards.
When Bwalya walked away to collect firewood, Monkey saw his chance.
“Why does fish have to weigh so much?” he complained.
Finally, with all his strength, he lifted the basket.
Monkey wanted to cross a small stream to reach the forest.
Inside, the fish slipped from side to side.
Monkey jumped around trying to catch them.
But the river carried them away.
Bwalya picked up a small cup.
Bwalya continued pouring water into it.
“A greedy heart is like this cup.”
“It does not know when to stop.”
For the first time, he understood.
He had been given something freely.
“Learning from mistakes is better than hiding them.”
The next morning, Bwalya came to the river.
To his surprise, Monkey was waiting.
Monkey pointed to the fishing nets.
And when the cooking fire was ready…
This time Monkey did not ask for everything.
Enough can make a person happier than too much.
Many years later, parents in the village still told children:
“Do not lose what you have because you are chasing what you do not need.”

lesson: Greed can make us lose our blessings. Learning to appreciate what we have brings happiness.
newWords: Greed – wanting more than you need
questions: Why did Monkey steal the fish?
Why did Bwalya share even after Monkey was wrong?
What does it mean to have enough?
Have you ever wanted more than you needed?

title: The Magic Drum

body.text: A Story About Kindness, Respect and Sharing
Many years ago, in a small village surrounded by forests and hills, people believed that everything in nature had a lesson to teach.
The rivers taught patience because they travelled slowly but always reached their destination.
The trees taught generosity because they gave shade even to strangers.
The sun taught faithfulness because every morning it returned.
And the elders taught children that kindness was the greatest treasure a person could own.
In this village lived a young boy named Tupole.
Tupole was not from a wealthy family.
His family did not have many cattle or large fields.
But Tupole had something many people admired.
Whenever an elderly person needed help carrying firewood, Tupole helped.
Whenever someone needed water from the stream, Tupole offered.
Whenever younger children struggled, Tupole encouraged them.
“My grandmother says kindness is like planting a tree.”
“You may not enjoy the shade today, but one day someone will.”
One year, the village experienced a terrible dry season.
The maize plants struggled to grow.
Every family had to be careful with what they had.
One evening, Tupole looked at his grandmother.
She only wanted him to eat.
That night, Tupole could not sleep.
“I must find a way to help,” he thought.
The next morning, Tupole woke up early.
He picked up a small basket.
Tupole walked deep into the forest.
After many hours, Tupole became tired.
He sat under a large old tree.
Until he reached a small clearing.
In the middle of the clearing was something unusual.
Traditional patterns were carved around it.
Pictures of animals decorated its sides.
“Because even when you had little, you still helped others.”
Drum of kindness, play your song, Bring the help we need along.”
Suddenly, the forest became filled with music.
The next day, they called the villagers.
The chief’s assistant, Kasonde, heard about the drum.
“If I get that drum, I can have everything.”
That night, while everyone slept, Kasonde followed Tupole’s footprints.
“A gift taken selfishly loses its power.”
A strong wind filled the room.
The next morning, Kasonde carried the drum back.
The village never forgot the magic drum.
But the greatest lesson was not about magic.
“The real magic was never inside the drum.”
“The drum only revealed what was already inside your heart.”
And from that day, whenever children heard drums playing in the distance, they remembered the story of Tupole.
A generous heart creates the greatest music.

lesson: A gift becomes more valuable when it is used to help others. Greed takes away joy, but kindness multiplies blessings.
newWords: Generosity – willingness to share with others
questions: Why did the drum choose Tupole?
Why did it stop working for Kasonde?
Should special gifts be shared?
What kindness can you show someone today?

title: Jelita and the Missing Library Book

body.text: Jelita loved Wednesdays because Wednesday was library day at Chisomo Primary School.

The library occupied one bright room beside the head teacher's office. It was not large, but to Jelita it felt bigger than the whole town. Its shelves opened doors to distant kingdoms, deep forests, great rivers and planets that shone beyond the night sky.
Her favourite book was The Moon over the Zambezi. It told the story of two children who followed the silver path of moonlight across the river to help a lost fisherman find his village.
Jelita had borrowed it twice. On Tuesday afternoon, she returned it through the wooden return box before hurrying to assembly.
On Wednesday morning, Mrs Phiri stood beside the library door with a worried expression.
"Before anyone borrows a book today, I need your help," she said. "The Moon over the Zambezi is missing. It was recorded as returned, but it is not on its shelf."
Jelita's stomach tightened. "I returned it yesterday, Mrs Phiri. I placed it in the box myself."
Mulenga, who had come to look for a book about bridges, noticed her concern. "Then the book must still be somewhere nearby," he said. "Let us help search."
Mrs Phiri agreed, but reminded them to handle every book carefully and return each one to its correct place.
Jelita searched the story shelves. Mulenga examined the return box and looked behind the librarian's desk. They checked under chairs, between encyclopaedias and inside a cupboard of old newspapers.
The book was nowhere to be seen.
Then Jelita noticed a thin trail of red dust. It began beside the return box and crossed the floor toward the reading corner.
"This dust came from outside," she said. "Someone with dusty shoes walked from the box to the atlases."
Mulenga lifted the heavy atlases one at a time. Beneath the last book, he found a torn borrowing card.
"Now we have a clue," he whispered. "But where is the book?"
A younger pupil named Tisa stood at the doorway. She held her schoolbag tightly and looked as though she wanted to speak, but every time Mrs Phiri glanced toward her, she lowered her eyes.
Jelita walked over without accusing her. "Hello, Tisa. Are you looking for a book?"
Tisa shook her head. "I came because? because I know something about the missing one."
They moved to a quiet corner. Tisa explained that she had found The Moon over the Zambezi inside the return box after assembly.
"I wanted to read it," she said. "But I was afraid Mrs Phiri would refuse. I still owe a fine because my little brother drew in another library book."
She had hidden the book behind the atlases, planning to ask about it later. When she returned that morning, it was gone.
Mulenga frowned. "Moving it without permission caused this confusion."
Jelita nodded, but her voice remained gentle. "Thank you for telling us. Now we can solve the problem together."
The three pupils told Mrs Phiri everything. Tisa's words came slowly at first, then rushed out all at once.
Mrs Phiri was disappointed, but she did not shout. "A mistake becomes harder to repair when we hide it," she said. "Telling the truth gives us somewhere to begin."
They returned to the reading corner. Mulenga searched beneath the woven mats. Jelita checked behind the low shelf. Mrs Phiri examined the windowsill.
A sudden breeze lifted several worksheets from a table and carried them through the open window.
Jelita looked outside. Pages lay against the fence, and one white sheet had caught beneath a flowering shrub.
"The wind!" she cried. "If the book was left near this window, perhaps the wind pushed it too."
They hurried outside. Beyond the shrub, hidden by long leaves, lay The Moon over the Zambezi. Its cover was dusty, but its pages were dry and undamaged.
Tisa apologised for moving the book and promised always to ask before borrowing.

Mrs Phiri explained that the damaged-book fine was meant to teach care, not to stop a child from reading. She arranged for Tisa to help dust shelves and repair book covers for twenty minutes each Friday until the fine was settled.
"You will still be allowed to borrow one book at a time," Mrs Phiri added, ?as long as you care for it responsibly."
Tisa's face brightened. She filled in a borrowing card and officially checked out The Moon over the Zambezi.
Before leaving, Jelita helped Mrs Phiri place a secure lid on the return box and move it away from the open window. Mulenga made a small sign reminding readers to return books properly.
That afternoon, Tisa sat beneath a jacaranda tree reading the opening page. Jelita and Mulenga passed her on their way home.
Jelita smiled. Finding the book felt good, but helping someone admit a mistake and remain welcome in the library felt even better.

lesson: Honesty and kindness make it easier to correct mistakes.
newWords: Library - a place where books are kept for reading or borrowing
Clue - something that helps solve a mystery
Admit - to tell the truth about something
Relief - comfort felt when worry has ended
questions: Why was Tisa afraid to ask for the book?
What helped the children find the missing book?
Was Mrs Phiri?s solution fair?
What should a reader do after making a mistake with a borrowed book?

title: Mulenga and the Flooded Footpath

body.text: Heavy rain drummed on the roofs throughout the night. It filled water drums, bent the tall grass and turned the dusty paths into ribbons of mud.
By morning, the stream beside Mulenga's village had grown wide and brown. Its usual gentle sound had become a deep, rushing roar.
Mulenga woke early because his class was presenting science projects. He had spent two weeks building a model bridge from thin sticks, string and carefully folded cardboard.
He wrapped the model in a plastic sack and held it against his chest.
At the mango tree, Jelita waited in her yellow blouse and navy skirt. She studied the dark clouds.
"My grandmother says the lower footpath floods after rain like this," she warned.
"We cannot be late," Mulenga replied. "My presentation is first, and everyone is expecting to see my bridge."
"A bridge model is not more important than a safe journey," Jelita said.
Mulenga did not answer. He was certain the stepping stones would still be visible.
When they reached the stream, the water was already flowing over the footpath. Only the tops of two stepping stones could be seen.
A broken branch spun in the current, struck a rock and disappeared downstream.
Mulenga tested the mud with one shoe. "If we move quickly, we can cross before the water rises further."
Jelita caught his sleeve. "Look at that branch. The current carried it away as if it weighed nothing."
Two younger pupils, Chipo and Temwani, arrived behind them. They were nervous, but when they saw Mulenga near the water, they stepped closer.
Mulenga realised that the younger children often copied him. If he attempted the crossing, they might follow even if he told them not to.
He remembered his father's advice: A leader's actions speak before his words.
Mulenga stepped away from the edge. "We are not crossing here," he announced. "We will use the upper road."
The upper road curved around a hill and added nearly an hour to the journey. Mulenga worried about his presentation, but the angry water had made the correct choice clear.
Before leaving, Jelita removed a bright red cloth from the top of her lunch basket. Mulenga tied it between two trees across the approach to the path.
They added branches beneath it so that anyone coming from the village would stop before reaching the flooded bank.
"We should tell an adult," Chipo said.
On the upper road, they met Mr Banda, a farmer guiding an ox-cart loaded with empty grain sacks.
He listened carefully when the children described the flooded crossing.
"You made a wise decision," he said. "Climb onto the cart, little ones. I will take you as far as the school junction, then alert the headman."
Jelita and Mulenga walked beside the cart because their muddy shoes would have dirtied the sacks. They helped push when one wheel sank into soft ground.
The journey was slow, but no one complained.
They arrived after the first lesson. Mulenga expected the teacher to be angry, but news of the flood had already reached the school.
Several pupils from other villages were also late. The presentations had been postponed until everyone arrived safely.
When Mulenga's turn came, he placed his model on the table. He explained how triangles spread weight and how strong supports protect a bridge.
Then he paused and told the class what had happened at the stream.

"My model stayed dry," he said, ?but I learned something more important than the facts in my presentation. A strong bridge helps people cross, but good judgement keeps them away when there is no safe bridge."
The class discussed how to warn families during floods. They painted signs showing a crossed-out stream and arrows pointing toward the upper road.
Community members inspected the crossing that weekend. They cleared blocked drainage channels and began planning a raised footbridge above the flood level.
At assembly, Mulenga received a special safety certificate. He felt proud, but not because he had won a prize.
He was proud because Chipo and Temwani had reached school safely.
On the way home, Jelita nudged him. "You were right about one thing."
"Your bridge project was important. It helped the whole community think about building a real one."
Mulenga smiled. He had discovered that courage did not always mean moving forward. Sometimes courage meant stopping, thinking and choosing a safer direction.

lesson: Real courage means choosing safety and protecting others.
newWords: Current - water moving in a particular direction
Risk - the possibility of danger or harm
Judgement - the ability to make a sensible decision
questions: Why did Mulenga first want to cross the stream?
Why did he finally choose the upper road?
What did the children do to warn others?
What is the safest response to a flooded crossing?

title: Jelita, Mulenga and the School Garden

body.text: The environmental club at Chisomo Primary School received a neglected patch of ground behind the classroom block.
The soil was hard, weeds reached Jelita's knees and part of the wire fence had fallen against an old stump.
The club teacher, Mrs Lungu, gave the pupils a challenge. "Turn this forgotten place into a useful garden before the end of the term."
Jelita imagined baskets of tomatoes, onions and leafy vegetables for the school kitchen.
Mulenga stretched his arms wide. "I will grow the largest pumpkin anyone in this district has ever seen."
On the first Saturday, nearly every club member arrived. They cleared weeds, loosened soil and planted seeds. By midday, neat beds covered the patch.
They celebrated as if the harvest had already arrived.
During the next two weeks, the garden began to struggle.
Some pupils forgot their watering days. Goats pushed through the weak fence and ate young leaves. The sun hardened the uncovered soil, and weeds returned between the rows.
Mulenga blamed the goats. Other pupils blamed the heat. One group accused another of using too much water.
Jelita opened the club notebook. The first page listed many exciting ideas, but no one had written who would complete each task or when it should be done.
"The weather is difficult," she said, ?but our biggest problem is that we started without a plan."
Mrs Lungu did not solve the problem for them. Instead, she asked, "What does a living garden need every week, not only on the first day?"
The pupils listed water, healthy soil, protection from animals, weeding and careful observation.
They formed teams. One repaired the fence with straight poles and stronger wire. Another collected dry grass for mulch. A third checked plants for pests.
Jelita created a picture schedule using symbols for watering cans, hoes, leaves and fences. Even the youngest members could see their duties.
Mulenga collected used plastic bottles, cleaned them and made tiny holes in the lids. He buried each bottle beside a plant so water would drip slowly toward the roots.
The first dripper emptied too quickly. The second barely released any water.
Mulenga adjusted the holes until the flow was steady. "An invention sometimes needs patience before it becomes useful," he said.
Jelita wanted straight planting rows because they were easy to measure and weed. Mulenga wanted curved beds that followed the slope and caught rainwater.
Their disagreement grew louder until Mrs Lungu asked a simple question: "How can you discover which idea works without arguing?"
They planted one small straight section and one curved section. After the next rain, the curved bed held more water, while the straight rows were easier to weed.
Instead of choosing one winner, the club combined the ideas. They used curved borders to slow water and straight inner rows for crops.
One evening, a gatepost came loose and three goats entered the garden.
A pupil passing nearby raised the alarm. Jelita, Mulenga and two neighbours guided the goats out without frightening them.
The pumpkin vine had been trampled, but its main stem was still alive.
Mulenga wanted to pull it out and start again. Jelita showed him a new green shoot beneath the damaged leaves.
They supported the vine with sticks, added compost around its roots and gave it time to recover.
Within weeks, yellow flowers opened along the stem.
By the end of term, the neglected patch had become a green outdoor classroom.
The club harvested tomatoes, rape, onions and beans. Mulenga's pumpkin was so heavy that two pupils carried it on a wooden board.
They sold part of the harvest and used the money to buy seeds and repair tools. They gave another part to the school kitchen and saved the healthiest seeds for the next season.
At the harvest celebration, Jelita pointed to the duty schedule, now marked with many completed tasks.
"The garden did not grow because of one brilliant idea," she said. "It grew because many people completed small responsibilities."
Mulenga placed a hand on the giant pumpkin. "It also grew because we tested our different ideas instead of trying to defeat one another."
The garden became a place where pupils studied soil, insects, nutrition, measurement and teamwork.
Long after the celebration ended, the bottle drippers continued their quiet work'one careful drop at a time.

lesson: Teamwork succeeds when people organise, cooperate and complete their responsibilities.
newWords: Mulch - material placed over soil to protect it
Schedule - a plan showing when tasks should happen
Harvest - crops gathered when they are ready
questions: Why did the garden struggle after the first Saturday?
How did the club organise the work?
What did Jelita and Mulenga do when their ideas differed?
Which action best demonstrates teamwork?

title: Jelita and Mulenga at the Science Fair

body.text: A colourful poster appeared beside the head teacher's office: DISTRICT SCIENCE FAIR?SIMPLE SOLUTIONS FOR EVERYDAY PROBLEMS.
Jelita read it twice. She had always wondered whether sunlight could preserve fruit without an expensive electric machine.
Mulenga wanted to build an alarm that warned families when a water container was nearly empty.
Their teacher, Mr Zulu, liked both ideas. Unfortunately, the school could send only one project team and provide one display table.
"Work together," he suggested. "A good team can sometimes discover a solution that neither person would find alone."
At their first meeting, Jelita drew plans for a solar food dryer. Mulenga pushed her paper aside to demonstrate a bottle, string and bell.
At their second meeting, Mulenga built a wooden frame while Jelita covered another box with clear plastic.
After a week, they had two unfinished models and very little cooperation.
Jelita's grandmother found them arguing on the veranda.
She listened quietly, then asked, "Whose problem are you solving?"
The next day, they visited families, the school kitchen and market traders.
A fruit seller explained that ripe bananas and mangoes sometimes spoiled before they could be sold, especially when rain kept customers away.
The school cook said fruit had to be washed carefully, but the cleaning container sometimes ran empty during busy mornings.
A farmer added that an invention would be most useful if local people could repair it with affordable materials.
Jelita filled several notebook pages. Mulenga stopped talking about which idea was better and began asking questions.
At the market, a trader named Auntie Ruth examined their drawings.
"Why must the dryer and water indicator be separate?" she asked. "Clean water is part of preparing safe food."
On the walk home, Jelita and Mulenga saw the connection.
They designed a solar dryer made from a wooden box, a clear sloping cover and screened trays. A small washable water container stood beside it with a floating marker that showed the water level.
Their first test took place on a bright Saturday. They washed banana slices, arranged them on the trays and placed the dryer in direct sunlight.
The inside became warm, but by afternoon the fruit was still damp. Drops of water covered the clear lid.
Mulenga looked around nervously. "We should not mention this test to the judges."
Jelita wrote FAILED?MOISTURE TRAPPED in their notebook.
"If we hide what went wrong, we will repeat it," she said. "Failure is information."
They asked Mr Zulu why the moisture remained inside. He did not give them the answer. He asked them to think about where damp air could escape.
They added screened vents near the bottom and top of the box. Warm air rose through the upper vent while fresh air entered below.
The second batch dried better, but slowly. They raised the trays and changed the angle of the clear cover to catch more sunlight.
They tested equal pieces of fruit, recorded drying times and asked Auntie Ruth to examine the final results.
"This batch is evenly dried," she said. "And insects cannot reach it through the screen."
On the morning of the fair, clouds covered the sky.
Mulenga worried that their solar dryer would appear useless. Jelita packed samples from earlier tests, their notebook and a small lamp that demonstrated how light entered the box.
At the exhibition hall, another team displayed a polished electric dryer with switches and bright lights.
The Jelita and Mulenga model looked simple beside it. Its wood showed pencil marks, and one corner had been repaired twice.
"It is made from materials people can find and repair," Jelita replied. "That is part of our solution."
When the judges arrived, Mulenga explained the problem reported by families and traders.
Jelita showed the first failed test, the trapped moisture in their drawing and every change they had made.
They demonstrated the floating water marker and explained why washing fruit and hands was important.
One judge asked, "What would you improve next?"
Mulenga suggested a stronger adjustable stand. Jelita proposed testing different screens and adding a simple rain cover.
The judges were impressed that the pupils understood their project's limitations instead of pretending it was perfect.
At the closing ceremony, Jelita and Mulenga received the Practical Innovation Award.
More importantly, Auntie Ruth and another trader asked the environmental club to help build larger dryers for the market.
On the bus home, Mulenga turned the certificate over in his hands.
"Your idea did not defeat mine," he said.
"And yours did not defeat mine," Jelita replied. "They became more useful together."
They opened a fresh notebook. On the first page they wrote a new question: What other everyday problem could be solved by listening first?

lesson: Good inventions grow from listening, testing and learning from failure.
newWords: Solution - an answer to a problem
Prototype - an early model used for testing
Evidence - information that helps show what is true
Innovation - a useful new idea or method
questions: Why did Jelita and Mulenga make little progress at first?
How did community interviews improve their project?
Why did Jelita record the failed test?
Which process is most likely to produce a useful invention?

title: Chisola and the Secret of Kifubwa Stream

body.text: Chisola noticed small details that other people often passed without seeing.
She noticed when the first mushrooms appeared after rain, when ants moved their eggs before a storm and when the Kifubwa Stream changed colour after a busy weekend.
One Monday, the water below the footbridge carried plastic wrappers and an oily rainbow shimmer.
"The stream looks unwell," Chisola told her friends at school.
Vumbi shrugged. "Perhaps yesterday's rain washed soil into it."
Bernice looked carefully. "Soil does not usually shine like that."

Their environmental-club teacher, Mrs Kankasa, warned them not to touch or taste unknown water. She gave them gloves, observation sheets and permission to investigate from safe public paths with an adult.
On Saturday, Chisola, Bernice, Vumbi, Wana, Chishomyo, Chiwape and young Chawana followed Mrs Kankasa along the stream.

They recorded what they saw without accusing anyone. Upstream, the water was clear. Near the market path, wrappers had collected against reeds. Farther down, rainwater flowed from a blocked roadside drain.
Chishomyo sketched a map. Wana counted pieces of litter in three equal areas. Bernice interviewed willing traders while Mrs Kankasa listened.
Most traders used bins, but strong wind scattered rubbish from an uncovered collection point. A mechanic showed them a leaking container that had already been moved away from the drain.
Vumbi wanted to announce that they had found the guilty person.
"We have found several causes, not one villain," Chisola said. "We must report what we observed accurately."
The children presented their notes to the market committee and local council representative.
They proposed covered bins, a regular collection day, drain clearing and signs explaining why waste should never enter the stream.
Adults handled the oily container and any unsafe material. The children wore gloves and collected ordinary litter from dry ground.
Chawana painted a blue stream on the first sign. Bernice added fish and reeds. Chiwape made everyone laugh by drawing a wrapper with running legs.
After the next rain, water moved freely through the cleared drain. The oily shine disappeared, although Chisola knew the stream would need continued care.
The club created a monthly observation walk. They compared photographs, counted litter and reported problems to adults.
At assembly, Chisola explained that protecting nature was not a one-day performance.
"The stream told us something was wrong," she said. "We helped because we looked carefully, gathered evidence and worked with the community."
From then on, whenever her friends hurried over the bridge, they remembered to pause and look at the water below.

lesson: Protecting nature begins with careful observation, reliable evidence and responsible action.
newWords: Evidence - information that helps establish what happened
Contamination - the presence of something harmful or unwanted
Responsible - acting carefully and accepting a duty
questions: What first made Chisola concerned about the stream?
Why did the children investigate with an adult?
Why did Chisola refuse to blame one person?
Which action offers the best long-term protection for the stream?

title: Bernice and the Storytelling Day

body.text: Bernice could turn an ordinary classroom into a moonlit village with only her voice.
When she described wind, listeners heard leaves rustling. When she imitated a proud chief or a frightened goat, even the teachers laughed.
The school announced a storytelling day. Each pupil could present a family story, an original tale or an account of local history.
Bernice wanted to win the audience prize. She remembered a beautiful story her grandmother had told beside the evening fire.
"I will perform Grandmother's story," she told Chisola. "Everyone will love it."
"Have you asked whether she wants it shared?" Chisola asked.
Bernice had not considered that question.
That evening, Bernice visited her grandmother and repeated the story's opening lines.
Her grandmother smiled, then became thoughtful. She explained that parts of the story belonged to their family, while another part had been learned from an older storyteller many years earlier.
"A story may travel," Grandmother said, "but a careful storyteller remembers the road it travelled."
She allowed Bernice to share the family section if she introduced its source. She asked her not to perform a short ceremonial song because Bernice did not yet understand its purpose.
Bernice felt disappointed. The song was the most dramatic part.
Grandmother offered another path. "Create your own ending. Let the old story give you a seed, but grow something honest from your imagination."
The next afternoon, the friends helped Bernice practise.

Wana listened for confusing parts. Chawana suggested that the lost child follow fireflies home. Vumbi wanted a chase through the forest. Chishomyo proposed a clever signal made with reflected moonlight.
Bernice combined the ideas but wrote the final words herself.
At storytelling day, she stood before pupils, parents and elders.
"The beginning of this story was shared with me by my grandmother," she said. "I am presenting it with her permission. The ending is my own."
She told of a child lost between tall trees, guided not by magic alone but by lessons remembered from home.
When she reached the omitted song, Bernice did not imitate it. She paused, described the respectful silence around it and moved into her new ending.
The room remained completely still until her final sentence. Then applause filled the hall.
Another pupil received the audience prize, but the elders gave Bernice special recognition for responsible storytelling.
Her grandmother hugged her. "Today you did more than entertain people. You respected the story and those who carried it."
Bernice later started a source page in her notebook. For every story, she recorded who shared it, whether she had permission and which parts she created.
She discovered that giving credit did not make her voice smaller. It made her storytelling more trustworthy.

lesson: Stories should be shared with permission, honesty and respect for their sources.
newWords: Source - the person or place from which information comes
Permission - agreement allowing someone to do something
Ceremonial - connected with a formal cultural occasion
Credit - public recognition of someone's contribution
questions: Why did Chisola advise Bernice to speak to her grandmother?
Why was the ceremonial song omitted?
How did Bernice make the performance partly original?
What should a storyteller do before sharing a family story publicly?

title: Chawana and the Injured Crowned Crane

body.text: Chawana was the youngest member of the school nature club and the first to arrive whenever an animal needed help.
One afternoon, she heard a weak flutter near a wet field beyond the garden.
A crowned crane stood among the reeds. One wing hung lower than the other, and a length of discarded string was tangled around its leg.
Chawana moved closer with both hands open.
"Wait," Wana said. "A frightened wild bird may injure itself or you."
"But we cannot leave it," Chawana replied.
"We will help wisely," Chisola said, "not hurriedly."
The children kept a safe distance and asked Chiwape to call Mrs Kankasa.
They stopped people and dogs from approaching, observed the bird's location and placed no food or water near it.
Mrs Kankasa contacted a local wildlife officer. While they waited, she explained that wild animals may have special diets, hidden injuries or diseases that untrained people cannot recognise.
Chawana worried that waiting meant doing nothing.
"Protecting the space is an important action," Mrs Kankasa assured her.
The officer arrived with a ventilated carrier, a cloth and protective gloves. He approached slowly, covered the crane to calm it and removed the string.
The wing was bruised rather than broken. The bird needed quiet observation before release.
The officer showed the children the tangled line. It had probably come from a torn sack or discarded parcel.
"Small waste can become a dangerous trap," he said.
Chawana remembered seeing loose string near the market and football field.
The club organised a safe litter survey. They used tools and gloves, and adults handled anything sharp or unknown.
Vumbi and Chiwape made collection frames for reusable cord. Bernice prepared a short assembly talk about securing string, fishing line and plastic loops before disposal.
Chishomyo designed covered collection boxes that prevented wind from carrying light waste away.
Three days later, the children watched from a distance as the recovered crane was released near the wetland.
It stepped cautiously, opened both wings and rose above the reeds.
Chawana wanted to run after it, but she remained still and let the bird choose its direction.
"I thought kindness meant touching it and making it better myself," she said.
Wana smiled. "Sometimes kindness means finding the person who knows how to help."
Chawana kept one grey feather the officer found in the empty carrier. She placed it beside the club's litter map as a reminder that compassion works best when guided by knowledge.

lesson: Helping wildlife safely means keeping a distance and contacting knowledgeable adults.
newWords: Wildlife - animals and plants living naturally in an area
Tangled - twisted together so that movement is difficult
Ventilated - designed to allow fresh air to enter
Compassion - concern for someone or something that is suffering
questions: Why did Wana stop Chawana from approaching the crane?
What useful action did the children take while waiting?
What had injured the crane?
What is the safest response to an injured wild animal?

title: Vumbi and the Dangerous Shortcut

body.text: Vumbi ran as though every path were a race and every journey had a trophy waiting at the end.
On the morning of the interschool football match, he promised to meet the team bus at the main road.
A fallen tree delayed traffic, and the coach sent a message saying the bus would wait only fifteen minutes.
"There is a forest shortcut," Vumbi told Chiwape. "We can reach the road before everyone else."
Wana shook his head. "That path is not part of our agreed route."
Vumbi had heard older boys mention it, but he had never walked it himself.
He ran into the trees. Chiwape followed because he did not want his friend to travel alone.
At first, the shortcut seemed clear. Then it divided beside a large anthill.
Vumbi chose the wider branch. Soon thick grass covered their shoes, and neither boy could hear the road.
Chiwape wanted to turn back, but every tree behind them looked the same.
Vumbi pretended not to be worried. "The sun is on that side, so the road must be ahead."
Clouds moved over the sun. They reached a shallow valley filled with wet ground and thorny plants.
Chiwape stopped. "We are lost. We need to use the safety plan from the club."
They stayed together, moved away from the wet ground and returned to the last place they clearly recognised: the anthill.
Chiwape blew the whistle attached to his schoolbag'three short blasts repeated after a pause.
Vumbi placed his bright football shirt on a high branch and resisted the urge to wander in search of help.
At the main road, Chisola noticed that Vumbi and Chiwape had not arrived.
Wana told the coach about the shortcut. Adults organised a search and contacted the boys' families.
Bernice called their names from the known entrance while an adult followed the path. Chishomyo listened for the whistle.
The answer came faintly through the trees.
The search group found the boys near the anthill. They were tired and embarrassed but safe.
Vumbi apologised for leaving the agreed route and for encouraging Chiwape to follow.
The team missed the first half of the match. Vumbi expected the coach to remove him completely.
Instead, the coach allowed him to sit with the substitutes and watch how the team communicated and followed instructions.
