So, that night, when all was quiet, the Moon took the gold-tipped spear for the third time. She managed to get out of the Jackal's house, but in the garden she fell over a bucket. The Jackal woke up but was not quick enough to catch the Moon this time, as she was already high up in the sky.

The gold-tipped spear had a magic power that enabled the Jackal to hunt successfully, but now, without it, he was helpless. He became thin and sickly, and the only food he got was the left overs from other animals' meals.
So, to this day, the Jackal climbs a hill at night and howls at the Moon to make her return his spear.

lesson: Jealousy and theft bring suffering to others.
newWords: Disguise - appearance used to conceal identity
questions: Why does Jackal howl at Moon?
source: Parvathi Raman, Kalulu the Hare and Other Zambian Folk-Tales (Arthur H. Stockwell Ltd., 1979)

title: The Wax-Maidens

body.text: There was once a woman, a hunter's wife, living in a little village, deep in the woods. She was very clever in making dolls and other figures out of clay, wood-gum or bees' wax. She used to give them away to little children in her village. During the rainy season, her husband would collect a number of honeycombs, and store the honey in earthen pots or gourds. The woman gathered the wax from the combs and used it for her own amusement.

Once she had gathered enough wax to mould two beautiful maidens, as large as real human beings. When the work was completed, she was herself so struck with their beauty and grace, that she wished intensely for them to come alive and sing and talk to her. In all her prayers to her ancestral spirits, she asked for this boon. Sure enough, the ancestral spirits listened to her plea, and the wax-maidens came alive. This was a great occasion for the whole village to celebrate. Life became very pleasant for the hunter and his wife, when they had these two daughters of their own.

After a long time, when everyone had accepted the wax-maidens as normal human beings, a young farmer from another village happened to see them, when they were sitting in the cool shade under a tree. Not knowing who they really were, he wondered that such wax-like, pale beauties could exist in the world. Full of admiration for them, he returned to his own village.

Since that day he could think of nothing else. He wondered if they were strange, beautiful spirits who haunted young men, or whether they were real human beings, whom one could marry. He was all the more thoughtful, because he was a married man, and wondered whether his first wife would allow him to marry more wives. But he was desperately in love with the two maidens and pined away thinking of them.

Observing his dejection, his first wife asked for the reason. Reluctantly he revealed to her what had happened. Being a dutiful wife, she gave him permission to marry the wax-maidens, on condition that they too shared in the housework and hard tilling work in the field, because she honestly believed that the wives could together greatly increase their wealth.

This was enough encouragement for the young farmer. He hastened to the wax-maidens' parents with his proposal of marriage. His status in life satisfied them. His straight and honest conduct won the parents' admiration. They agreed to celebrate the marriage, when the young farmer paid them eight head of cattle, four goats and six hens as the 'Lobola' or the bride-price for the much valued wax-maidens.

However, the parents warned him that their daughters were delicate creatures, who should be treated very gently. They should not be allowed to work in hot and sunny places, nor allowed to exert themselves too much. If he neglected this warning, they would melt away. In his over-eagerness to marry them, the foolish young farmer agreed to this condition. However, he did not reveal this truth to his first wife, for fear that she would scold him for marrying useless women, and prevent the marriage.

After the ceremony, the young farmer proudly brought his beautiful brides home. The moment they set their feet in the house, the first wife realized what a tremendous mistake it was. The maidens looked so dainty that she knew they had never done any housework at all. Their hands were so soft and sleek, they were utterly unfit for hard work in the fields. They walked so straight, that they could never carry loads on their heads nor babies on their backs.

What a waste of the 'Lobola'! Besides, she noticed day by day, they were both in great dread of the fire. They refused to cook food on the hearth and always preferred to eat cold things. They avoided long exhausting walks and generally became tired all too soon. Most of all, they would never venture out into the open, sunny fields to do the important work of the farmer. For a few months the first wife tolerated this dainty nonsense, and carried on with all the chores, single handed. Soon however, the additional work of catering for the lazy women proved too much for the simple woman. It was infuriating. While she toiled away like a mule, the two pale creatures enjoyed the cool comfort of the house.

Tearfully, the bitter woman complained to her husband about the attitude of his new wives. The foolish man only laughed, because it suited him perfectly to have two beautiful women to entertain him with sweet songs and talk, while a hard-working woman looked after all the other chores in the house. He never explained to her the reason for their laziness, but carried on without paying any heed to his first wife's complaints.
Seeing her husband's heartless behaviour, the first wife confided in her neighbours, who advised her to use her wit to extract work from the lazy women, when the husband was not in the house.

Since that day, she pretended to be kind to the wax-maidens in her husband's presence, but when he was away, she set hard work for the girls to do. She demanded obedience, as the first wife, and supervised all their chores untiringly. But the hard work severely told on the poor helpless creatures. The waxen beauty began to wear from their face and hands, they became lean and listless. Nevertheless, the revengeful wife drove them into the field to till the land. The elder one ran to the field. In great alarm, the younger maiden begged for mercy, because she feared her sister would surely melt away in the hot sun.
"Nonsense," retorted the first wife, "no woman ever melts away by working in the sun."

Under the midday sun, the elder maiden actually began to melt. The wax dripped down from her body and ran on the soil. The young sister watched helplessly, because she could not go to her rescue. By evening she had melted so much that only a big toe from her foot remained on the field. In the cool of the evening, the young one ventured out to collect the toe and placed it in a pot of cold water. Not wishing to stay in the house any longer, she went to her mother's house, lamenting her sister's fate.

When the young husband returned in the evening, his first wife was still enjoying her leisure, believing the wax-maidens to be at work. But the food was not cooked, the field was not tilled and the wax-maidens were nowhere to be seen.

Frantic with anxiety for the safety of his beloved wax-maidens, the young husband ran to the village of the maidens, only to learn the sad news, and to see the only remaining wax toe of the beauty. Due to the long walk and her heavy heart, the young sister too had melted into a grotesque lump of wax, beyond anyone's recognition.
Tearing off into the dark night, an anguished cry escaped the lips of the distracted husband, as he blindly ran into the woods, never to return.

title: A Different Baby

body.text: This story took place a long time ago, when strange things used to happen off and on. In those days a man and his wife lived in a country full of happy people. The couple had four healthy sons, but they yearned for a little daughter. When the wife was expecting their fifth child, they hoped it would be different this time, a girl child, for example. The man and his wife prayed day and night, repeating the same words, "Please, God, make it different this time, make it different this time."

They could not say anything else. When finally the day came, when the mother went into labor, the father fell on his knees, requesting all the Gods and Spirits to remember their prayer, and make it different.
In a few hours' time the mother was safely delivered of a handsome baby, and an old nurse brought the news to the father.
"Glad news, master," she informed him politely, "it is, indeed, different this time."
"Different?" gasped the father in exultation. "God be thanked a thousandfold!"
"Yes, different," announced the old woman solemnly, "the lady of this house has just given birth to a handsome little puppy dog!"

"What?" The father was at first greatly shocked at this news. He stood petrified for some time, but when once he set eyes on the cute little puppy dog, all his anger vanished, and his heart melted with tender love for the soft, helpless creature.

Days went by and all the family cherished the little puppy dog, because of his lovable, gentle nature. He followed his elder brothers wherever they went, and guarded his father's home and property with devotion. Even as a baby, he was no trouble to his mother, as he was the most obedient child anyone could ever want. All the world adored him.

When the boys grew up to be strong, handsome young men, the father bade them to seek their fortune in the wide world, on their own merit, because, he said, it would not be manly for them to stay protected in the parental home any more. He gave them good advice and his blessings.
Later, he also gave each of his sons a hoe, and a sharp knife with which to fend for himself. The mother tied up some food in five identical bundles for them and sent them on their way.

Now the little puppy dog had grown up to be a very strong animal, almost resembling a lion, but his nature remained as gentle as before. As he could not carry his hoe and his knife and his bundle of food, his elder brothers carried them for him.

After various encounters, the young men at last arrived at the country of a good Chief. They presented themselves before the Chief and requested him to try their skill. The Chief was much impressed by their fearless, yet courteous bearing, and so, he employed them to lay a path leading from his palace to the river. Thus the cargo from the boats could be transported into the palace yard easily.

This was a distance of about fifteen miles or over. In those days, it was a great distance indeed. Yet, without a murmur, all the brothers set to work immediately, in unison. In a very short time they laid a very good passable path, on which carts, cattle, horses and men could carry their goods with comfort.
While the work was going on, the little dog guarded the possessions of his elder brothers and protected them from wild animals.

It was only a test to prove their skill. No need to say, they passed it with great honours. By some strange coincidence, the Chief had five beautiful daughters, whom he wanted to give away in marriage to deserving young men. The four elder brothers proved to be the best choice any parent could make as suitors to his daughters. Without a moment's hesitation, the Chief offered his four elder daughters in marriage to the four elder brothers.

When the ceremony was going on, someone was very unhappy. This was none other than the Chief's youngest daughter, Nalishebo. She was very disappointed that she could not find a husband from among the hard-working brothers. Thinking it to be a joke, the elder brothers offered their puppy dog as her companion. The girl accepted the dog, and looked after him carefully.

As the Chief was growing old, he gave a portion of his land to each of his daughters and bade them to lead a peaceful life. Now was the real time for competition among the elder brothers. They vied with one another in cultivating their respective lands and growing different types of produce. They built roomy huts and homes for their families. They hunted many animals and procured warm skins. They had, in short, much to eat and drink and enjoyed a bounteous life.

Nalishebo alone was left out. Being a fragile young maiden, she could not do all the work a man would do. As a result, she could hardly keep her hut clean, let alone, cultivate the land. She was tired and ashamed to have to borrow food and skins from her father or her sisters. One day she was far too dejected about her situation and spoke bitterly to the poor dog.
"Look at all my sisters," she remarked, venting her wrath on him, "they have good strong men to help them. But what have I got? Only a worthless dog who can only eat and sleep!"
The poor dog could only whine sympathetically and wag his tail.

Next morning, when Nalishebo woke up and looked out of her hut, a great surprise awaited her. As if by some strange power, the weed had been completely cleared from her land. At the back yard, several rows of newly dug beds were laid ready for planting seeds. Nalishebo wondered who could have done this good work for her.

All her sisters came to see the work. There was much guessing and much talking, but none could find out who did all the work. Day after day passed, each morning bringing new reason for wonder to the young girl. One day fresh thatch was laid on the roof, the next day all land was tilled, on the third morning saplings were planted and on the fourth, there were blossoms everywhere. Nalishebo imagined she was living in a dream-land. Even her sisters and their husbands left off teasing her, because they could not, themselves, make their lands flourish so well. They even suspected that there was some spell, good or bad, working on Nalishebo's land. Many nights they kept watch to catch the worker red-handed. But all their efforts were in vain.

Once, at dead of night, Nalishebo suddenly woke up to hear the noise of someone tilling the land. She quietly slipped out of her hut. In the dim moonlight she could see a young man bent over his work, in deep concentration. She had never seen any one of that stature in the neighbourhood. Her heart pounding with excitement and fear, she approached the man to have a closer look. She took a few steps forward, but suddenly she stepped on something soft and warm. As she bent down to examine the object, she screamed, "Oh my pet, my dear dog is dead!" and tearfully she gathered the animal in her arms. Strange to say, it felt very light.
Her scream alerted the working young man. He came running to her, "Please, give me back my skin, quick!" he urged.

At once everything became clear to Nalishebo. The handsome young benefactor was none other than the dog himself. By some magic power, this young man could get in and out of the dog skin, as he chose! He had been keeping this power a secret for many years, but Nalishebo accidentally discovered it that night.
The young man begged Nalishebo not to divulge the secret to anyone, because if many others knew of of it, his power would wane and he would be condemned to remain a dog for ever.

Such things could not be hidden from prying eyes for long. As her sisters and others suspected that she entertained a secret lover, the young girl thought of a plan to bring the matter to the open, at least to protect her own good name. In those days it was considered very important that the daughters of the Chief set an exemplary example for the other maidens of a chiefdom. If Nalishebo was proved to be a wanton maiden, she could be punished severely.

Nalishebo realized that the secret of the young man would be out some day and he would be condemned to be a dog for ever. On the other hand, if she protected the secret much longer, the Chief and the elders of the country would punish her for her wayward behaviour.

Therefore, when next time the young man came out of the dog skin at night, she crept up behind him to steal the skin. When he was hard at work, she burned the dog skin to ashes. It was a pity, though, to have to destroy such a smooth, healthy, lovely skin that she adored all along. This she had to do, in order to retain the young man in his human form for ever, and to extricate herself from the false stories.
In this way, Nalishebo broke the spell, and married the fifth young brother, and they all lived happily ever after.

lesson: Loyalty and character matter more than outward appearance.
questions: How was the fifth baby different?
source: Parvathi Raman, Kalulu the Hare and Other Zambian Folk-Tales (Arthur H. Stockwell Ltd., 1979)

title: Why the Lion Roars

body.text: Long ago Lion's voice was as quiet as that of a lamb. This allowed him to catch and eat the other animals without warning. One day all the animals gathered to find a way to stop his cruelty. They talked for a long time but found no answer.

At last Hare had a clever idea. "I shall change his voice into a mighty roar," he said. "Then we will always know when he is coming." The animals agreed, and Hare began his difficult task. He went to Lion and said, "My lord Lion, someone is very ill and wishes to see you."

"Where is he?" Lion asked. "Follow me and I will take you to him," Hare replied. Hare led Lion deep into the bush. Lion became tired and lay down beneath a tree, where he soon fell asleep. A hive of bees was nearby. Hare took honey from it and smeared it all over Lion's body while he slept.

When the bees returned and saw that their honey had been stolen, they became furious. They found Lion covered in honey and attacked him. Their stings caused such terrible pain that Lion awoke with a thunderous roar. He roared so much that his gentle voice was changed forever.
To this day the animals thank Hare for his cleverness, for whenever Lion approaches they hear his roar and run away.

title: Why Ostrich Has a Long Neck

body.text: Long ago, before Ostrich had a long neck, Crocodile and Ostrich were friends. The other animals warned Ostrich, It is foolish to be Crocodile’s friend." But Ostrich had a large head and very little sense, and would not listen.

One day Crocodile was extremely hungry, having eaten nothing for many days. He said, "Friend, my throat is sore. Put your head into my mouth and see where it hurts." Foolishly Ostrich obeyed. Crocodile closed his jaws and bit Ostrich’s head.

Ostrich pulled and pulled until at last he escaped, but all that pulling stretched his neck very long. Crocodile finally released him, and Ostrich fled in terror. From that day he has lived only in swamps and small streams, always watching for crocodiles.

lesson: Choose friends wisely and listen when others warn you about danger.

title: Why Chickens Scratch the Ground

body.text: Have you ever wondered why chickens continually scratch the earth? They are always searching for something. This is the reason. Long ago, before the hornbill could fly, he was a close friend of the chickens. One day he obtained a beautiful, valuable needle with which he could sew his clothes.

The chickens saw their friend flying gracefully high in the sky and wanted to do the same. They begged, "Please lend us your needle. We want to make wings like yours." Hornbill answered, "No. You may lose it, and then our friendship will end."

The chickens promised to guard it carefully. At last Hornbill lent them the precious needle and warned them once more not to lose it. Soon one careless chicken used it and misplaced it. Hornbill and all his relatives became angry and began hunting chickens.

"From this day," they said, ?you will be our prey until you find our needle." That is why chickens still fear birds of prey and begin scratching whenever one appears. They are searching for the bright needle that they lost long ago.

title: Why Frog Says Croack-Croack

body.text: Long ago Frog spoke as clearly as a bird. One day Frog and Mouse were walking together when they found a cooking rack with a fine piece of meat upon it. Mouse said, "Let us eat it before its owner returns. You climb up and taste it while I watch the path."

"Very well," said Frog, ?but watch carefully and warn me when the owner comes." Frog climbed up, tore off a delicious piece and put it into his mouth. The owner soon approached. Mouse was frightened and ran away without warning his friend.

Frog could think of nothing to do but pretend to be asleep. The meat in his mouth was extremely hot and burned him, yet he dared not chew, spit it out or cry out, for the owner would see him. He held it in his mouth until the owner finished eating and left.
That night Frog tried to speak as before, but the hot meat had badly burned his mouth. He could only make the sound ?mbototo-mbototo." From that day to this, that is all he has been able to say.

title: Why the Hyena Laughs

body.text: Long ago Hyena was walking across the plain in high spirits when he met his friend Hare. "Master Hare," Hyena said, ?what news have you for me today?" "Well," Hare replied, closing one eye, "I saw a strange little animal today."

Hyena asked, "What was it like? Did it have a tail or horns?" Hare said, "It had neither, but its legs were extremely long." "My goodness! What did it look like?" cried Hyena. Smiling, Hare continued, "It could change itself into many shapes - a tall person, a short one, a fat one or a thin one."

Hyena stared at the ground and asked, "Were its eyes like ours?" "Not at all, friend," said Hare. "One eye looked straight ahead while the other looked sideways." This description amazed Hyena. He burst into uncontrollable laughter and ran away.
Even today, when you hear Hyena laughing in the night, you may know that he is remembering Hare's absurd animal. Can you guess what creature Hare described? It was a human being!

title: Why the Hare Drinks Dew

body.text: One day Hare was drinking dew from the leaves of a tree. Tortoise, who was nearby, asked, "Why do you do that? Why not drink from the river as the other animals do?" Hare replied, "To tell the truth, I have never thought about it.

Since drinking dew is troublesome, I shall do as you say." He hurried to the river, bent his head and began to drink. Then he saw his own reflection in the water and thought another hare was already there. He drew back angrily and said, "I will never drink from a pool or river again, because my relatives have filled them all."
From that day Hare has kept his promise. He drinks only the morning dew, and his drinking place is still upon the leaves of the trees.

title: How Hippo Lost His Horns

body.text: Many years ago, when Hippo lived on dry land, he was a very handsome animal. He had magnificent golden horns, long and beautifully curved like those worn in the ancient land of Persia. All the animals wished for horns like his, except one jealous little creature with a very long nose.

That animal decided to trick him. One day he found Hippo and said, "Master Hippo, today is very hot and you are sweating. I do not think you dare to bathe in that pool, because you are afraid the gate that holds your horns may not keep them in place beneath the water."

Hippo replied proudly, "My horns are perfectly secure." At once Hippo plunged into the cool pool. The water was so refreshing that he dived and rolled about in it. But the water loosened his horns and washed them away'splash!
Ashamed and angry, he remained in the pool to hide. Thus the long-nosed animal outwitted him. To this day Hippo lives in cool river water, still mourning the beautiful horns he lost.

title: Why the Hyena Walks with a Limp

body.text: Have you noticed how Hyena seems to limp when he walks? It happened because Hare played a cruel trick on him. One day Hare and Hyena were travelling together. Hyena laughed and said, "How badly you walk! Perhaps your legs are crooked."

Hare pretended to be hurt, then asked, "Will you do something to help me?" "Certainly," Hyena replied. Hare said, "Close your eyes and walk backwards. Continue until I tell you to stop." Foolish Hyena obeyed. Walking backwards with his eyes shut, he fell into a very deep hole.
His legs were badly injured, and from that time he began to limp. He has never walked properly since, because Hare punished him for his mockery.

title: How Birds Learned to Speak

body.text: Long ago birds and bats were friends. In those days neither birds nor bats could fly, and neither could speak as they do today. Both groups suffered greatly because human beings kept them as servants. At last they met and said, "Why should we continue suffering merely because we cannot fly?

Let us ask our Creator for help." Their Creator listened and said, "I will consider your request." When they returned the next evening, he said, "I shall give you wings." He gave wings to both the birds and the bats. The birds were delighted and sang songs of thanks to their Creator.

The bats, however, forgot to thank him. For their ingratitude, the Creator separated them from the birds and allowed them to fly and speak only in darkness. That is why bats fly and call only at night, while birds sing by day in gratitude to the one who freed them.

title: Why Fish Live in Water

body.text: Long ago fish lived on land with the other animals. They did not live well with their neighbours, for they delighted in mocking the other creatures, comparing one animal with another and causing quarrels. At last all the animals of the forest refused to tolerate their gossip.

They caught the fish and cut out their tongues so that they could no longer make mischief. Then they carried them to the riverbank intending to kill them. During the night the fish slipped into the water and escaped. They decided that it was safer to remain there.

Their wounded tongues became small, so they could no longer gossip. Yet they were happy, because from then on they could not stir up quarrels among the other creatures in the river. That is why fish live in water and do not speak.

title: Why Porcupine Has Spikes

body.text: Porcupine was once a very proud animal. He was also handsome and loved hearing the other animals praise his beauty. One day he boasted to Hyena, "If every animal were as beautiful as I am, the world would be a splendid place."

Hyena was offended and began thinking of a way to humble him. Hyena said with a laugh, "Listen, sir. In that thorny grove lives someone who can make you even more beautiful. Go and ask him. But first leave your fine coat with me, so that it will not be spoiled."

Foolish Porcupine did as he was told and entered the thorn bushes. The thorns scratched his whole body, and he could not free himself. Hyena laughed and said, "You cannot wear your beautiful coat over those ugly stripes.
I shall wear it myself." So Hyena kept Porcupine’s soft and handsome coat, while Porcupine was left with a rough coat marked by dark stripes. From that day he could boast of his beauty no longer.

title: Why the Owl Flies at Night

body.text: Many years ago all birds and animals believed Owl to be extremely wise. Whenever a dispute arose, they brought it to Owl so that he might judge it. One day Hare asked him, "Master Owl, which is the wiser: a white chicken or a black one?"

Owl answered, "That is easy. The black chicken is wiser, because it can lay a white egg, while the white chicken cannot lay a black egg." "Thank you, Master Owl," said Hare. "If you are so wise, can you lay a black egg?"

Owl confidently said that he could and went away to try. But no matter how hard he tried, only a white egg appeared. Deeply ashamed, Owl thought, "How can I face the animals after claiming that I could lay a black egg?" He hid until darkness fell.
Since that day Owl has flown only at night, hiding his embarrassment from the other animals.

title: Why Tortoise Has a Hard Back

body.text: Tortoise was the last of all the animals to be created. By then the Creator had used nearly every part, so the animals gathered their leftovers for him. They gave him a tongue like a lizard's, a birdlike beak and nose, a head shaped like a snake's, and front legs unlike his hind legs.

Even so, Tortoise was content and lived peacefully among the others. One day Chameleon asked, "Friend, why are you so ugly?" Tortoise replied, "I may look ugly, but my flesh tastes better than that of any other animal." Chameleon could not keep a secret and spread the news everywhere.

When the animals heard that Tortoise had delicious flesh, they began hunting and eating his people. The Tortoise found no escape from the hunters, so they begged a tree to protect them. The tree agreed and grew a hard covering of bark over their bodies.

Thus they gained strong shields. To deceive their enemies, each one travelled alone, pretending that another Tortoise was close behind. Eventually their trickery made them distrust one another, and they scattered. That is why Tortoise has a hard back and why two of them are seldom seen walking together.

title: Why the Cat and Dog Quarrel

body.text: Long ago people kept Cat and Dog together in their houses to guard their possessions. One day a man who owned both animals told them to let no one enter while he was away. He left a large piece of fat meat on the table and ordered them to guard it.

As soon as the man had gone, Cat began eating the meat. When the owner returned, it was gone. He asked sternly, "Who ate it?" Cat quickly answered, "I do not know. Perhaps a stranger took it while Dog and I were outside."

Dog became angry at the lie and said, "That is not true. I saw Cat eating it. Look'there are still pieces of meat around his mouth." The owner seized Cat and beat him. Cat was furious with Dog for exposing him. He chased him away, crying, "If I ever see you again, I shall bite you!"
Since that day Cat and Dog have been enemies.

title: Why the Elephant Fears the Mouse

body.text: It seems strange that a creature as huge and powerful as Elephant should fear Mouse, but it is true. Some say Elephant thinks Mouse may crawl into his trunk and block it. Here is another explanation. Many years ago Elephant had a painful wound in his leg that would not heal.

One day Mouse found him exhausted with pain. "Master Elephant, what is wrong?" Mouse asked. Elephant told him about the wound. Mouse examined it and said, "I can help you." He began treating and cleaning it. After several days it had still not healed, and Elephant promised to reward Mouse for every object Mouse removed from the wound.

Whenever Mouse asked for payment, Elephant told him to search again, and the treatment continued for a long time. Now whenever Elephant sees Mouse, he becomes afraid, thinking that Mouse has come to demand the reward still owed to him.

title: Why the Giraffe Has a Long Neck

body.text: Long ago Giraffe had short legs and a short neck like Rhinoceros. One day Giraffe met his friend Rhino and complained about hunger. Rhino agreed and said, "So many animals feed on the ground that little food remains. The leaves high in the trees are still fresh.

Let us ask the wise Man to help us reach them." They found the Man and explained their trouble. He laughed and said, "That is easy. Come tomorrow at midday and I shall give you special herbs. When you eat them, your legs and necks will grow long enough to reach the treetops."

The next day only Giraffe arrived. Rhino forgot the appointment. The Man gave Giraffe the promised herbs, and when he ate them his legs and neck grew very long. He could now reach the sweetest leaves at the tops of the trees.

Rhino arrived later and was angry to discover that all the medicine had been given to his friend. He believed the Man had deceived him and has remained bad-tempered ever since. Whenever Rhino sees a person, he charges. Giraffe, however, still enjoys the tender leaves that his long neck enables him to reach.

title: Why Leopard Has Spots

body.text: Long ago Leopard had a plain body like Lion's. He was unhappy and wished that his skin could be bright and attractive like that of other animals. He kept this desire hidden in his heart. One day he met Snake. Snake said, "Leopard, I am suffering and feel very ill.

Please examine me." Leopard replied, "You are a dangerous and angry creature, so all the animals fear you. But since you are ill, I shall help." He examined Snake and treated him until he recovered. Snake was very grateful and said, "Ask for anything you desire."

Leopard replied, "I want a beautiful, brightly patterned body." Snake said, "I can change you. I shall bite you, but do not be afraid that you will die. The bites will spread over your body and become spots." Snake bit Leopard, and his whole body became covered with beautiful markings.
They became close friends and have remained so ever since.

title: Why Monkeys Resemble People

body.text: Many years ago no rain fell, and famine came upon the land. The people gathered all the food that remained and hid it in one place, appointing trustworthy men to guard it. One day they discovered the guards eating the food.

Everyone was furious and brought the men before the chief. The chief said, "You will run into the forest in shame because you have stolen our food. I shall not kill you, but I shall punish you in a way you will never forget.

I will turn you into animals that resemble people. Human beings will chase you from their villages, and you will live in trees and eat wild fruit." He changed them into monkeys. Ashamed, they fled into the forest. That is why monkeys resemble human beings.

title: The Friendship of Pulu and Ngolo

body.text: If you travel through the bush, you may see Pulu and Ngolo together, for they are close friends. One day Ngolo asked the animals to help him kill Crocodile, who had eaten many of their companions. The animals refused, saying, "We are afraid of Crocodile."

At last Pulu said, "I will help if you follow my plan." Ngolo asked what he intended to do. Pulu replied, "We shall drink all the water from the pool. Then we will be able to see Crocodile and kill him." Ngolo agreed, and together they began drinking.

Clever Crocodile saw what they were doing, slipped quietly from the shrinking pool and fled toward a large river far away. Pulu and Ngolo followed, caught him, bit him and trampled him again and again. Crocodile's soft skin was badly wounded.

Great rough scales rose wherever they had injured him. He eventually escaped into the river, but his body had been changed. From that day Pulu and Ngolo have remained friends. When they go to drink, they first look carefully around, because Crocodile still waits for a chance to catch them and avenge the damage they did to his skin.

lesson: Friends can achieve difficult things when they work together.

title: Why Collared Dove Has a Ring Around His Neck

body.text: Chameleon was not always as brightly coloured and beautiful as he is today. One day he saw birds wearing feathers of many colours and wondered where they had obtained them. The birds told him, "Ask Collared dove. He knows where beautiful colours are kept."

Chameleon found Collared dove and asked for help. Collared dove said, "I will help you. Come to me when you see a rainbow, and I will take you there." When a rainbow appeared, Chameleon returned with several beetles who also wanted new colours.

Collared dove said, "Hold on to one another around my neck so that I can carry you to the rainbow." They did so, and Collared dove took them there and rolled upon the colours. Chameleon received many beautiful colours, and so did some of the beetles.

But in their excitement none of them released Collared dove's neck before they left. Their tight grip made a lasting ring around it. Collared dove did not mind, because everyone heard that he had helped Chameleon become beautiful.

lesson: Helping others can leave a lasting mark of honour.
